frase_gancho.texto: A huge fan of feathers for dancing the history of the Conquest.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave Oaxaca and continue toward the Gulf Coast, the land of the Huastec and the Totonac. Look for a garment with two points, embroidered with flowers and brightly colored birds.

guion_corto.texto: The Danza de la Pluma is danced in the Central Valleys of Oaxaca. It is part of the festivals of the patron saints and of the Guelaguetza, the great festival of July. With steps and music, it tells the story of the Conquest of Mexico: on one side, Moctezuma and his people; on the other, Hernán Cortés, his soldiers, and La Malinche. The costume is recognized by its headdress, a fan-shaped crown. It is made of colored feathers on a light base and is fastened to the head with a band. It carries ribbons and ornaments that shimmer as the dancer moves. The dancer also usually carries a metal rattle that marks the rhythm. It is a large, heavy headdress, and dancing with it takes balance and strength.

guion_largo.texto:
In the highlands of Puebla, you saw a crown that spins like a sun. Here you come to the other great feather dance I told you about: the Danza de la Pluma. The headdress changes, becoming a fan. And the story changes, speaking of the Conquest of Mexico.

It is danced in towns of the Central Valleys such as Cuilapam de Guerrero, Zaachila, San Bartolo Coyotepec, Teotitlán del Valle, and Zimatlán. According to the Smithsonian, it reaches at least seventeen communities. It almost always forms part of the festival of the patron saint. San Bartolo Coyotepec may sound familiar: it is the town of black clay. The dance also travels. Since the 1980s, organizations of migrants from Oaxaca have taken it to the United States.

The dance represents the Conquest. On one side are Moctezuma and his warriors; on the other, Hernán Cortés, Pedro de Alvarado, and the Spaniards. La Malinche also appears. For the INAH, the dance tells the Conquest from an Indigenous point of view. It speaks less of a defeat than of the blending of cultures from which today’s Mexico was born. Moctezuma is the king whose supposed headdress you see in the Mexica Hall.

Where does it come from? There is no single answer. Its birthplace is usually placed in Cuilapam de Guerrero, although Zaachila also claims it. It is often repeated that Dominican friars created it in the sixteenth century. But some researchers doubt this and ask for documents. Some link it to older dances. What is certain is that today it is a very much living tradition.

Look closely at the costume, because it is not made by just one person. Behind each one, several crafts are at work: the person who prepares the feathers, the one who shapes the metal base, the one who weaves the clothing, and the one who carves the hand-held objects. The headdress is assembled with a metal base, a light frame of river cane, colored feathers, and ribbons. It is large and heavy, and for that reason the one who wears it dances with a firm back.

In towns like Teotitlán del Valle and Cuilápam, the dancers are young people who commit for several years. Afterward the headdress passes to a new group. The music is played by a wind band, with clarinets, tuba, and drums. What is curious is what they play: waltzes, polkas, schottisches, and marches. They are melodies with no known author that are learned from generation to generation. A sixteenth-century story told with European ballroom rhythms.

Every July, on the Cerro del Fortín in the city of Oaxaca, the Guelaguetza is celebrated. It is the Zapotec word you already know: to give in order to receive. The Danza de la Pluma is the culminating moment of the traditional Guelaguetza. For several dance masters, it is part of the heart of their identity.

Feathers, which in ancient Mexico marked rank and wealth, adorn these headdresses today with a very different meaning from the original. Before moving on, look for the fan, the ribbons, and the hand-held objects of the costume. And think about how many hands it takes for a story from almost five hundred years ago to keep being danced.

texto: Look for the headdress: is it shaped like a fan or a half circle?
Notice the ribbons and the ornaments that hang or shimmer
Look for the hand-held objects, such as the rattle that marks the rhythm

texto.Culture: Zapotec of the Central Valleys of Oaxaca (Cuilápam de Guerrero, Teotitlán del Valle, and Zaachila)
texto.Period: Viceregal tradition and living contemporary tradition
texto.Material: Semicircular headdress of river cane, dyed feathers, mirrors, silk ribbons, tin rattle, and bracelet

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Danza de la Pluma is a pre-Hispanic dance that has been danced the same way since before the Conquest.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It tells the story of the Conquest, with Moctezuma, Cortés, and La Malinche. Its exact origin is debated, and some specialists see it as a tradition formed after the Conquest.
